procedural_history.originating_court: NCDRC (National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission) - inferred from the text mentioning C.C.No.945 of 2019 and the Supreme Court closing the right of the Respondent to file a written statement in the proceedings before the NCDRC.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order passed by the High Court. The High Court incorrectly observed that reopening the suit by setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree would be futile because the defendants had not filed a written statement.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court reviewed an order from the First Appellate Court that set aside an ex-parte judgment and decree. The High Court did not comment on the correctness of the First Appellate Court's decision on its merits. The High Court incorrectly stated that reopening the suit would be futile because no written statement was filed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants approached the Supreme Court because they disagreed with the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court ruled that while the Respondent-builder could not file a written statement in C.C.No.945 of 2019, they could participate in the proceedings. The Supreme Court also held that the Respondent is bound by the earlier Order of the Supreme Court, and could have not been permitted to introduce its case through written submissions. The objections raised by the Respondent cannot be looked to the extent it carried pleadings, which could have been let in through a written statement.

directions: The C.C.No.945 of 2019 shall now be proceeded further without the written statement of the respondent-builder.
It shall however, be open to the respondent-builder to participate in the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party whose right to file a written statement is closed can file written submissions to introduce pleadings to resist the claim against it.

facts: A prior Supreme Court order had closed the Respondent's right to file a written statement in the proceedings before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC).
Despite this order, the Respondent attempted to introduce its case, pleadings, and objections through written submissions.
law: Drawing from the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and the judgment in Nanda Dulal Pradhan & Anr. vs. Dibakar Pradhan & Anr., the Court established that even when the right to file a written statement is forfeited, a party is not barred from participating in the proceedings.
This participation includes the right to cross-examine the other party's witnesses.
However, a party cannot introduce evidence for a case that has not been set up in the pleadings.
Therefore, the closure of the right to file a written statement bars the party from indirectly introducing its pleadings or case through other means, such as written submissions.
application: The Court found that the Respondent was bound by the earlier order that closed its right to file a written statement.
Allowing the Respondent to introduce its case and defense through written submissions would be an indirect way of circumventing the previous order.
The Court ruled that the pleadings and objections raised by the Respondent in its written submissions could not be considered, as they should have been part of a formal written statement.
The Respondent's right to participate was limited to cross-examining the complainant's witnesses and arguing legal questions based on the evidence presented by the complainant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Respondent's attempt to introduce pleadings through written submissions. It held that a party whose right to file a written statement is closed cannot use written submissions as a backdoor to introduce its case. Their participation is limited to cross-examining the opponent's witnesses and making legal arguments based on the existing record.

issue.issue_text: What is the scope of participation in the proceedings for a party once the right to file a written statement has been closed.

facts: The Supreme Court had previously passed an order closing the Respondent's right to file a written statement in proceedings before the NCDRC.
Despite this order, the Respondent was permitted to participate in the proceedings.
The Respondent then attempted to file written submissions that contained pleadings and objections, effectively introducing its case to resist the claim.
law: The Court relied on the principle that 'what cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly.'

Referencing the Code of Civil Procedure and the judgment in Nanda Dulal Pradhan & Anr. vs. Dibakar Pradhan & Anr., the Court affirmed that even when the right to file a written statement is forfeited, a party is not disentitled from participating in the proceedings.
The forfeiture of the right to file a written statement does not automatically mean the complainant wins; the complainant must still establish their case.

There is a legal distinction between forfeiting the right to file a written statement and filing one that fails to deny specific facts. In the latter case, undenied facts can be taken as admitted, but this does not apply in the former.
application: The Court found that the Respondent's written submissions were an improper attempt to indirectly introduce pleadings that should have been in a written statement, which violated the Court's previous order.

The Court clarified that the Respondent's permitted participation was limited. The Respondent had the right to cross-examine the complainant's witnesses and argue legal questions based on existing laws and authorities.
The Respondent could also make arguments regarding lapses or the non-admissibility of the evidence presented by the complainant.
However, the Respondent could not use written submissions or any other forum to bring in its own pleadings or evidence to support its case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a party whose right to file a written statement has been closed can still participate in the proceedings, but this participation is limited. The party has the right to cross-examine the opponent's witnesses and make legal arguments on points of law or the admissibility of evidence. However, they are barred from introducing their own pleadings or case facts, either directly or indirectly through written submissions.

issue.issue_text: Whether the forfeiture of the right to file a written statement makes it obligatory for the adjudicating body to pass an order in favour of the complainant.

facts: A party in a proceeding before the NCDRC (National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission) had its right to file a written statement forfeited.
law: The forfeiture of an opposite party's right to file a written statement does not, by itself, obligate an adjudicating body to rule in favor of the complainant.
The complainant still has the burden to establish their own case on its merits.
The power to require the complainant to prove their case, even in the absence of a defense, is an inherent part of the jurisdiction of any adjudicating body.

There is a legal distinction between the complete non-filing of a written statement (due to forfeiture) and filing a written statement that fails to deny specific allegations. In the latter case, the undenied facts can be taken as admitted, but this does not apply to the former.
application: The Supreme Court applied this principle to the NCDRC.
It reasoned that even though the respondent's right to file a written statement was forfeited, the NCDRC was not automatically required to find for the complainant.
The complainant was still required to prove their case, and the NCDRC had the power to assess the merits of that case independently.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the forfeiture of the right to file a written statement does not make it obligatory for the adjudicating body to pass an order in favour of the complainant. The complainant must still independently establish their case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a party whose right to file a written statement is closed can file written submissions to introduce pleadings to resist the claim against it.
appellant_arguments: The respondent, whose right to file a written statement was closed by a prior Supreme Court order, should not be permitted to introduce its case and pleadings through written submissions, as this would circumvent the order.
respondent_arguments: The right to participate in the proceedings should allow the respondent to introduce its defense and resist the claim through written submissions, even if the right to file a formal written statement has been forfeited.

arguments.issue_text: What is the scope of participation in the proceedings for a party once the right to file a written statement has been closed.
appellant_arguments: The scope of participation should be limited and should not allow the respondent to introduce a defense that ought to have been raised in a written statement.
respondent_arguments: The right to participate in proceedings should be interpreted broadly, allowing the party to effectively defend itself against the claim.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the forfeiture of the right to file a written statement makes it obligatory for the adjudicating body to pass an order in favour of the complainant.
appellant_arguments: The respondent's failure to file a written statement means the facts pleaded in the complaint should be taken as admitted, obligating the adjudicating body to rule in the complainant's favor.
respondent_arguments: Even without a written statement, the complainant still has the burden to prove their case on its own merits, and an order in their favor is not automatic or obligatory.

cases.principle: A party could not make out a case on the basis of evidence for which he/she has laid no foundation in the pleadings.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A party whose right to file a written statement has been closed by a court order is barred from introducing pleadings or its substantive case through alternative means, such as written submissions or objections, even if permitted to otherwise participate in the proceedings. Furthermore, the due date for handing over possession of a property must be determined strictly in accordance with the specific clauses of the governing agreement, not by an alternative method devised by a tribunal.
obiter: The rules of pleadings mandate that no pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A party whose right to file a written statement has been forfeited by a court order cannot be permitted to introduce its case and pleadings through the guise of written submissions. This is an impermissible circumvention of the court's order, as the principle of law is that what cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly. While such a party retains the right to participate in the proceedings, that participation does not extend to letting in pleadings that should have been in the forfeited written statement.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of law that what cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's appeal was allowed, however, their argument that the forfeiture of the right to file a written statement obligates the adjudicating body to automatically pass an order in their favour was rejected. The court implicitly affirmed that the complainant still has the burden to prove their case on its own merits.
why_respondent_won: Although the respondent's written submissions were disallowed, the respondent succeeded in securing the right to continue participating in the proceedings. The court's final direction explicitly states that 'It shall however, be open to the respondent-builder to participate in the proceedings,' thereby protecting this fundamental right despite the procedural default.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning upholds the finality and enforceability of its own orders. Allowing a party to defy a specific direction (closing the right to file a written statement) by introducing the same material under a different name ('written submissions') would undermine the authority of the court and the procedural framework.
